title: Bugatti Is Open to Building a Lightweight Tourbillon with a Stick

body_markdown:
Rimac and a group of New York City-based investors have shared ownership of Bugatti since[Porsche sold its stake in the brand](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/porsche-sells-stake-in-bugatti/) in April 2026. This is the first time in nearly 30 years that Bugatti isn’t linked to the mighty Volkswagen Group. Not being tied to a big corporation gives Bugatti more freedom, according to Rimac founder Mate Rimac, and his team has wild plans for the future.


Speaking to *[Top Gear](https://www.topgear.com/car-news/interview/we-can-do-bold-things-bugatti-might-do-a-lightweight-v16-tourbillon-a-manual)* , Rimac explained that[the V-16–powered Tourbillon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bugattis-next-chapter-the-tourbillon/) (which was developed to replace the Chiron; pictured) is more of a platform than a car. The version that’s scheduled to enter production in the not-too-distant future will look pretty much like the model unveiled in 2024, but Bugatti already has several offshoots in the pipeline. That’s hardly a surprise: Even when it was owned by Volkswagen, the company released numerous one- and few-off variants of its cars, such as[the Divo](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bugattis-type-35-hits-the-targa-florio-with-the-divo-for-old-times-sake/) and[the Mistral](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/2025-bugatti-mistral-for-sale-broad-arrow-auction/) .


“Now with the freedom, having the company independent from any car manufacturer, we can really think long-term and do bold things. And we will do lots of cool stuff,” Rimac told *Top Gear* . One of the ideas floating around the executive’s mind is a lighter, simpler version of the Tourbillon. Could it come with a manual gearbox instead of an automatic? “Absolutely. You bet,” he replied.


If the project reaches production, it would be Bugatti’s first stick-shift since[the Italian-made](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/wandering-the-hallowed-abandoned-halls-of-the-bugatti-eb110/) EB110 retired in 1995. The model was[exclusively available](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/eb110-at-30-the-bonkers-90s-supercar-that-revived-bugatti/) with a six-speed manual transmission, but all of Bugatti’s 21st-century cars have been automatic-only.

“I think the Tourbillon, as it is now, made a lot of sense as a successor to[the Chiron](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2022-bugatti-chiron-super-sport-review-obsessively-excessive/) . It’s an incredible car. But I wonder myself, what’s next for Bugatti, and what would be interesting to do? And I think light weight and simplification of stuff. Instead of a sledgehammer as Bugattis were \[in\] the last 20 years, could you do something that’s also more engaging, more back to the roots, more[Type 35](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/100-years-ago-bugatti-tore-up-the-rule-book-with-the-type-35/) ? There’s so many ideas,” Rimac told the publication. It sounds like he’s describing an even more hardcore[Bolide](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bugatti-bolide-validation-testing/) .


None of Bugatti’s modern road cars have qualified for the “lightweight” label. The hybrid Tourbillon weighs about 4400 pounds. It’s powered by a mammoth, 8.3-liter V-16 linked to a hybrid system that includes a 25-kilowatt-hour battery and a pair of electric motors. *Top Gear* speculates that Bugatti could achieve Rimac’s vision by removing the hybrid system and building a gas-only variant of the Tourbillon. The engine contributes 1000 horsepower to the total 1800-horse output, so it certainly wouldn’t be slow.


Rimac stopped short of confirming whether that’s what he has in mind. It sounds like the company has plenty of ideas, however.
